# Before the City Wakes

Before the city wakes, it belongs to the people who clean it. Windows shine in long yellow rectangles, revealing vacuums, mops, and the patient choreography of floors swept before sunrise. A baker opens a metal door and the smell of warm bread slips into the street, delicate at first, then impossible to ignore. Somewhere a bus exhales, its doors folding open like the ribs of a metal animal. The crossing signal changes, though no one is there to obey it. For these few minutes, the city is less a machine than a stage being prepared: curtains rising, lights warming, chairs.

At six, commuters appear, carrying the quiet focus of people who have not yet spoken much. They walk with their eyes lowered, not necessarily sad, but concentrated on the difficult arithmetic of being awake. One woman counts bus connections on the back of her hand. A man in a blue jacket buys a newspaper he will not read, because possibility is sometimes enough. Another person stands outside a closed flower shop, looking at the dark window as if plants might be sleeping behind the glass. They are not late yet. They are not early either. They are on time.

The bakery becomes a small theater of appetite. A schoolgirl orders a bun with sugar and a future she cannot see. An old man takes his usual coffee, black, and the clerk saves him the change before he reaches for his wallet. They exchange a nod built over years, an entire language with no need for grammar. At the corner table, a man eats alone, turning pages of a book whose story has slipped away unnoticed. He chews, reads, gazes out, and chews again, equally content to be lost, surrounded, and hungry in a city that has barely begun moving.

Across town, a park holds its breath. Birds test the branches, performing brief concerts for an audience of no one. A sprinkler clicks on out of sight and lays a crescent of rainbow over the grass. The benches are damp, but the man sitting on one has brought an umbrella and accepts the condition of things. I pass him each morning, and sometimes imagine our small consistency: the same path, the same hour, the same unspoken agreement that the day remains undecided. That possibility feels like a door left open in the mind. It closes quietly before I can enter.

By seven, the city has acquired its familiar masks. Coats become uniforms; umbrellas become armor; paper cups become the crowns and scepters of hurried kings. Doors open and close, open and close, carrying us in soft waves toward our separate labors. A taxi pauses beside a puddle, and for a moment the driver and passenger study the same reflection: two strangers folded into one bright shape. Then the light changes, and one of them is moving while the other remains. We are always being briefly mirrored by people we will never notice, life touching its double before the next turn.

Somewhere a child is being dressed for school, negotiating socks as if civilization depended on them. Somewhere an argument is folded carefully into a kitchen, quiet enough to spare a sleeping relative its dignity. Somewhere a letter is sealed, not because the words are finished, but because the writer has suddenly understood something. I used to imagine mornings as empty rooms, waiting for events to furnish them. Now I think mornings are already crowded: full of preparations, invisible maintenance, decisions without witnesses. Most of what holds a day together never becomes a story, and that is part of its kindness.

Traffic thickens into argument, a red river pushing impatient metal across the avenues. A delivery van stops for a cyclist who is already sorry for making anyone late. The cyclist waves. The van driver lifts two fingers off the wheel. Neither knows the other’s name, but their exchange is complete, a little civic grammar passed between strangers. On the sidewalk, a woman balances coffee, phone, and a paper bag of peaches with the concentration of a surgeon. A peach begins to roll free, hangs on the edge, waits. She catches it without looking, an expert in the laws of gravity.

At nine, offices glow with the pale electricity of modern captivity, everyone inside appearing to work while the windows keep their own bright count of ghosts. Streets that were sleepy now carry small armies of urgency, each person armed with a phone and the conviction that being contacted is not the same as being present. A man eats lunch at a bus stop, watching traffic dissolve into heat. A woman paints her nails in the rearview mirror of a parked car, careful not to smear the small red landscape of her patience. Nearby, a child draws a house with enormous windows.

By noon, the city has surrendered its freshness. The air thickens, gathers odors of asphalt, perfume, hot engines, and lunches eaten too quickly. Shadows shorten into hard shapes, and every surface seems to demand something: shade, payment, attention, a decision. A fountain continues its useless music for a square that needs it, perhaps most of all. A man reads under a tree, losing his place more than once, beginning again with patient embarrassment. I envy him, though I do not know his book. That is perhaps what makes admiration so easy: it can be borrowed without conditions of any kind.

Evening arrives without ceremony, announcing itself first in window light, then in the lengthening shadows of buildings. The city softens, but does not sleep. Kitchens begin to glow; plates clatter; someone somewhere laughs too loudly at something unexpectedly funny. The park empties slowly, as if its visitors are reluctant to leave a version of themselves behind. A bus returns, carrying tired bodies and the warm recollection of places just passed. I sit by the river while the water carries the light in pieces. Tomorrow will bring errands, missed words, unexpected surprises. It will bring the light. Tonight, more than enough.
